title: AIM: Attributing, Interpreting, Mitigating Data Unfairness

problem.claim: Real-world data can encode historical discrimination, creating unfairness that must be traced and addressed at the sample level.

gap.claim: FairML research has focused mainly on mitigating bias in model predictions, with less attention to tracing biases present in data.

contributions.claim: The paper investigates discovering training-data samples that reflect biases or prejudices.
The paper defines a sample bias criterion and proposes algorithms to measure and counter sample bias.
The paper develops two FairML strategies based on sample-bias-informed minimal data editing.

stated_novelty.claim: The authors explicitly describe discovering bias-reflecting training samples as a novel research problem.

author_reported_evidence.claim: The derived bias score provides sample-level attribution and explanation of historical bias in data.
The proposed strategies can mitigate group and individual unfairness with minimal or zero predictive utility loss.
Experiments and analyses on multiple real-world datasets demonstrate the reported effectiveness of the methods.

narrative_sequence.summary: Real-world data may contain historical discrimination against disadvantaged groups and individuals.
Existing FairML work emphasizes prediction-bias mitigation more than tracing data bias.
The paper frames discovery of bias-reflecting training samples as a research problem.
It introduces a sample bias criterion, measurement and countering algorithms, and two minimal-data-editing strategies.
The authors report sample-level explanations, unfairness mitigation with minimal or zero utility loss, and effectiveness across multiple real-world datasets.

source_observation.claim: The approach uses sample-level bias attribution before applying minimal data editing.

interpretation.claim: Tracing problematic data instances may support more targeted fairness interventions than modifying predictions alone.

application.claim: For fairness audits, consider identifying and explaining biased samples before selecting data-editing interventions.

exception.claim: The abstract does not establish when sample-level editing is preferable to other fairness interventions or how it behaves outside the reported datasets.

unknowns: The abstract does not specify the fairness notions, bias-score formula, or algorithmic details.
The abstract does not report dataset names, quantitative results, baselines, or experimental conditions.
The abstract does not establish independent verification, reproducibility, or the scope of generalization.
